case_name: The Public Guardian and Trustee of British Columbia v. Johnston
text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

The Public Guardian and Trustee of
British Columbia v. Johnston,

2016 BCSC 1388

Date: 20160726

Docket:
S143617

Registry: Vancouver

Between:

The
Public Guardian and Trustee of British Columbia,

as executor of the last will of Norman Johnston, deceased

Plaintiff

And:

David
Johnston, Mary Woodward, Thomas Johnston

and the Faith Fellowship Baptist Church

Defendants

And:

Jack Taylor, Faith Fellowship Baptist Church, The Public Guardian
& Trustee of British Columbia, Steven Miller, The Attorney General of
British Columbia,

Norman Johnston aka Norman Johnston, Deceased

Defendants by Counterclaim

Before: The Honourable Madam Justice Ballance

Reasons for Judgment

Counsel for the Plaintiff and Defendant

by Counterclaim:

D.
Manson

Counsel for the Defendant

David Johnston:

J.
Dubas

Counsel for Defendant by Counterclaim

Stephen Miller

S.
Cordell

Counsel for Defendants and Defendants by Counterclaim
Faith Fellowship Baptist Church and Jack Taylor

N.
Safarik

Place and Date of Hearing:

Vancouver,
B.C.

June
22 and September 8, 2015

Place and Date of Judgment:

Vancouver,
B.C.

July
26, 2016

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The late Norman Johnston was predeceased by his
wife, Barbara Johnston, both of whom were survived by their only child, David
Johnston.  For ease of reference and without intending disrespect to any party,
I will refer to the members of the Johnston family by their given names.

[
2
]

David is a defendant and has brought a counterclaim
in relation to this multi‑faceted estate litigation claim.  The
applications before the Court concern the pleadings he has filed.

FACTUAL OVERVIEW

[
3
]

On February 22, 2007, Norman and Barbara
executed mirror‑image wills (together, the “2007 Wills”) under which they
left their entire estates to each other, with a gift over to David on the death
of the survivor.  The testamentary gift to David was an outright bequest of the
residue of his parents’ joint estate, without conditions or the imposition of a
trust.  At that time and continuing until Norman's death, the Johnstons’
principal asset was their house in Vancouver which they owned as joint
tenants.  Accordingly, when Barbara died, title to the home passed to Norman as
the surviving joint tenant.  In his pleadings, David refers to this property as
the “Family Residence” and for convenience, I will do the same.

[
4
]

Stephen Miller is a lawyer who acted for Barbara
and Norman over the years, including with respect to the preparation of the 2007
Wills.

[
5
]

Barbara died on January 18, 2010, without having
revoked her 2007 will.  Soon afterward, Norman signed a power of attorney
document prepared by Mr. Miller in favour of David.  He subsequently suffered
a stroke.

[
6
]

In April 2010, Norman was temporarily admitted
to the psychiatric ward at Vancouver General Hospital, and was eventually placed
at the George Derby Hospital for veterans.  Amidst allegations implicating misconduct
on the part of David, the police were involved in Norman's removal from the Family
Residence and his admittance to hospital.  David complains that he was actively
prevented from seeing his father from that time until July 2013.

[
7
]

On or about June 10, 2010 Norman was certified
as being incapable of managing his affairs by way of a certificate of
incapability pursuant to the
Patients Property Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996,
c. 349 [
PPA]
.  In the result, the Public Guardian and Trustee of
British Columbia (the “PGT") became the committee of Norman's estate.

[
8
]

David had resided in the Family Residence for most
of his adult life and was living there when the PGT assumed committeeship of
his father's estate.  The PGT eventually determined that Norman would not be
returning to the Family Residence.  In July 2010, the PGT’s office informed
David that the Family Residence would be sold and that he was to vacate those
premises to facilitate the sale.  David resisted the PGT's proposed course of
action and was ultimately permitted to continue living in the Family Residence.

[
9
]

In the summer of 2012 or thereabouts, Mr. Miller
received instructions from Norman for the preparation of a new will.  Unbeknownst
to David, on September 11, 2012 and while Norman was still subject to the
certificate of incapability and a patient under the
PPA
, Norman executed
a new will (the “2012 Will").  Mr. Miller prepared the 2012 Will and
he, together with his legal assistant, witnessed its execution.

[
10
]

The provisions of the 2012 Will, summarized
below, differed significantly from Norman’s 2007 will:

a)

The PGT is appointed as the executor of the 2012
Will and trustee of the trusts constituted thereunder;

b)

Norman's personal articles, including any boats,
motor vehicles and domestic and household items, are to be distributed in
accordance with a memorandum and, subject thereto, given to David, other family
members or charities in the discretion of the PGT;

c)

A
legacy of $500 is bequeathed to each of Norman's sister-in-law and
nephew;

d)

A gift
of $5,000 is made to the Faith Fellowship Baptist Church (the
“Church”) for use by the Women's Missionary Circle; and

e)

T
he residue of Norman's estate is directed to be held in a
discretionary trust for David's lifetime.  Under the terms of the trust, the
income and capital of the trust property are available for David's care,
maintenance, education and benefit in the discretion of the PGT, and upon
David’s death, the remainder is distributable to the Church.  If the Church is
not then in existence, the residue of the trust property passes to The
Fellowship of Evangelical Baptist Churches in Canada (the “Fellowship of
Churches”).

[
11
]

On October 24, 2013, Norman executed a codicil
to his 2012 Will by which he increased the legacy to the Church from $5,000 to $100,000.
Mr. Miller prepared the codicil and once again he and his legal assistant
acted as the witnesses.

[
12
]

I will refer to the 2012 Will and Norman’s codicil
together as the “Impugned Wills”.

[
13
]

Norman died on October 28, 2013 at the age of
93, without having revoked or altered the Impugned Wills.  David is the sole
intestate heir and the only person entitled to apply to vary the Impugned Wills.

[
14
]

On about October 29, 2013, David filed a caveat to
prevent the issuance of probate of the Impugned Wills.  The caveat alleged,
among other things, that his father lacked the requisite testamentary capacity
and/or was subject to undue influence in relation to the preparation and
execution of the Impugned Wills.

[
15
]

On May 12, 2014, the PGT commenced this action seeking
an order that the Impugned Wills be pronounced for in solemn form of law (the
“Proof of Will Action”).  The defendants are David, Norman's sister-in-law, his
nephew and the Church.  The Church supports the relief sought by the PGT in the
Proof of Will Action and seeks dismissal of the Counterclaim.

[
16
]

It is not clear why the Fellowship of Churches
is not joined as a defendant. I will leave that potential oversight for counsel
to address.  In the meantime, I have determined that the apparent omission does
not hamper my ability to decide these applications, as the interests of the
Church and the Fellowship of Churches in respect of them are virtually
identical.

[
17
]

David's amended response to the PGT's notice of
civil claim (the “Response”) spans some 32 pages in length and contains a
rambling mixture of allegations of fact, evidence and argument.  David has also
filed an amended counterclaim (the “Counterclaim”) by which he joins Jack
Taylor, who is the Minister of the Church, the Church, the PGT, Mr. Miller,
the Attorney General of British Columbia and Norman’s estate as defendants.  In
addition to adopting the facts set out in the Response, the Counterclaim sets
out 11 additional pages of allegations, some of which are confusing or
problematic in other ways.

NATURE OF THE APPLICATIONS

[
18
]

The Response and Counterclaim form the subject
matter of the within applications.

[
19
]

With respect to the Response, the PGT seeks the
following:

a)

The Response be struck, with leave to file
within 21 days a substitute further amended Response that complies with the
Supreme
Court Civil Rules
, B.C. Reg. 168/2009 [
SCCR
] and the terms of this
Order;

b)

In the alternative, the Response be severed from
the Proof of Will Action and stayed;

c)

In the further alternative, the vast majority of
the paragraphs of David’s Response, which the PGT asserts offend various rules
of pleadings or have bearing on claims that extend well beyond the Proof of
Will Action, be struck or amended; and

d)

An order prohibiting David from taking any
further steps in this litigation until his Response has been substituted or
amended.

[
20
]

With respect to the Counterclaim, the PGT
requests that:

a)

It be severed and stayed as against the PGT
pending the outcome of the Proof of Will Action; and

b)

In the alternative, it be struck.

[
21
]

Mr. Miller asserts that the claims against
him as defendant by Counterclaim are bad in law and should be dismissed or
struck, with special costs.  Alternatively, he urges that all claims against
him in the litigation be severed and stayed pending the determination of the
Proof of Will Action and the balance of David’s claims relating to his late
father’s estate.

[
22
]

David opposes both applications.  Minister Taylor,
the Church and the other defendants by Counterclaim (except for Mr. Miller),
filed no materials in respect of these applications and did not appear at the
hearing.

DAVID’S PLEADINGS

[
23
]

Some paragraphs of David's Response and Counterclaim
contain
vague
and repetitive allegations,
other parts, particularly of the Response, are replete with evidence and
argument, and still others are a flawed mingling of such shortcomings.  Overall,
David’s Response is unduly drawn out and even discursive at times, and both
pleadings are laden with extraneous and collateral content.  The deficiencies are
serious and hinder the Court’s ability to accurately discern certain of David's
defences and claims.

[
24
]

As best I can determine, the principal allegations
in David’s Response, loosely organized by subject matter, are as set out below.

•

Proof of Will Action

[
25
]

David asserts that the Impugned Wills were made
under suspicious circumstances, and are invalid and of no force and effect on
the grounds that, at the relevant times, his father lacked the requisite testamentary
capacity, was suffering from delusions and was subject to duress and undue
influence exerted by Minister Taylor, the Church, Ms. Miller and others.

•

Misrepresentations, Pressure, Influence and Advice

[
26
]

David pleads that in the summer of 2010, members
of the PGT staff told him that his father did not wish to see him and to sever
contact.  He alleges that the PGT, Mr. Miller, the Church, Minister Taylor
and/or agents on their behalf, similarly made false representations to Norman
to the effect that David did not wish to see him and posed a danger to him.  David
claims they ultimately pressured Norman to make an “improper” decision not to
see him.  He alleges that the foregoing actions made his father more vulnerable
to the untrue suggestions voiced by Mr. Miller and members of the PGT
staff in “an unfair and undue way”.

[
27
]

It is not made clear whether these allegations
are confined to David’s claim that the Impugned Wills and the inclusion of the discretionary
trust are the product of duress and/or undue influence.

[
28
]

David goes on to allege that, in the event the
content of the Impugned Wills and, in particular, the imposition of the
discretionary trust, were derived either from the advice or influence of
counsel or others, such as members of the PGT staff, Mr. Miller, Minister
Taylor, the Church or of Norman’s own doing, in an attempt to avoid or limit
the application of the
Wills Variation Act,
the Impugned Wills should be
considered as being against public policy and declared void.  The rationale, in
his words, is that the use of the discretionary trust to convey his inheritance
under the Impugned Wills:

“... unfairly
and improperly is a colourable attempt which places the desires of these
parties and [Norman] ahead of the primary obligations of [Norman] to David and
on this basis the [Impugned Wills] should be declared void or varied such that
David receives the Family Residence and the net movable property of [Norman]
unconditionally as his sole property.”

•

Unjust Enrichment and Breach of Agreement
Concerning Mutual Wills and Breach of Corresponding Promises and Trusts

[
29
]

David claims that he performed many tasks and
functions for and on behalf of his parents throughout their respective lives,
and in doing so, directly and indirectly enriched them to his detriment.  He alleges
that he conferred such benefits on the firm understanding, pursuant to an
agreement and in keeping with their common intention that the surviving parent would
leave him the Family Residence, together with the remaining joint estate, free
from the imposition of a trust or other dispositive restrictions.

[
30
]

David pleads that, in pursuance of this
contractual and/or trust arrangement, his parents agreed with one another and promised
him that title to the Family Residence would belong to him outright.  Expanding
along similar lines, he alleges that he and his parents had an oral agreement
to the effect that Norman would transfer and vest title to the Family Residence,
as well as all other movable property, in David and that in exchange, David and
his mother provided Norman with benefits.

[
31
]

Tied to these allegations is David’s claim that
the 2007 Wills constitute mutual wills that were deliberately made by his
parents to capture and bind them to the foregoing arrangement.  David's
position is that the Impugned Wills were made by his father in violation of his
father’s agreement with Barbara upon which the 2007 Wills were fastened, and in
breach of the companion trust obligations and promises repeatedly made directly
to David.  He avers that because the 2007 Wills are mutual wills in law, it was
not open to Norman to change or revoke his 2007 will.

[
32
]

Accordingly, alleges David, the Impugned Wills
are void based on the doctrines of unjust enrichment, constructive trust,
resulting trust, express trust and breach of contract and ought not to be
admitted to probate.  He further claims that in consequence of the application
of these legal principles, beneficial ownership of the Family Residence ought
to be vested solely in his name, irrespective of the limitations imposed by the
Impugned Wills.

•

The Impugned Wills Constitute a Fraudulent
Conveyance

[
33
]

David asserts that the Impugned Wills have
defeated, hindered and delayed the dispositions promised to him by his parents and
thus are void in law and equity, and pursuant to the
Fraudulent Conveyance
Act,
R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 163 [
FCA
].  Additionally, he alleges that on this
basis, the Impugned Wills are against public policy generally and should not be
admitted to probate.

•

Claims Pertaining to Barbara's Estate

[
34
]

Also included in the Response are criticisms of
the actions allegedly taken by the PGT in relation to Barbara's estate.  His
complaints focus largely, although not exclusively, on what he alleges was an
excessive valuation placed by the PGT upon the cottage that Barbara and David
owned jointly, which has given rise to a capital gains tax liability payable by
David.

[
35
]

In the Counterclaim, David pleads and relies on
the facts alleged in his Response and reiterates many of them in one fashion or
another.  He also rephrases and expands upon his claims against the Church, the
PGT and Mr. Miller alleging:

a)

To the extent that Minister Taylor, the Church, Mr. Miller
and/or the PGT “induced or advised or contributed" to Norman making the
dispositions contained in the Impugned Wills for the purpose of defeating the
applicable wills variation provisions and thereby defeating or impairing the
entitlement of David under that legislation and/or “his natural entitlement” to
receive his father's net estate, the Impugned Wills are void for repugnancy.

b)

Mr. Miller, Minister Taylor, members
of the Church (for which the Church is responsible) and the PGT staff (for
which the Attorney General is responsible) exaggerated to Norman the problems
encountered by David stemming from his learning disability, and told Norman
things that were untrue, causing Norman to refuse to see David.  He alleges
that they falsely and without proper consideration for the consequences to
David, unfairly told Norman that David was a threat to him and as such they
unfairly and in a negligent fashion and in breach of their fiduciary
obligations “owed” to “him”, barred David access to his father for over two
years.

David alleges their misconduct caused him “much anguish and
suffering” and seeks damages for the “negligent infliction of suffering and
harm” based on the foregoing.

c)

In paragraph 16.1 of the Counterclaim, David
attempts to address the existence of a duty of care owed by Mr. Miller.  Specifically,
he alleges that Mr. Miller was retained:

“at various times to deal with estate
matters for [Norman, Barbara], and/or [David] or these people due to their
interactions with [Mr. Miller] were a class of people which he knew or
ought to have known were relying on his advice and actions as their solicitor.  In
the context of this relationship, [Mr. Miller] owed these three people a
duty of fidelity and a duty of reasonable care in his interactions related to
them at all times"

d)

He goes on to allege that, through these
interactions, Mr. Miller knew or ought to have known about the agreement
and trust obligations linked to the mutual wills

and

regarding
the ultimate disposition to David of his parents’ assets more generally.  Mr. Miller
was therefore precluded from taking any action that would defeat such
agreements or obligations (i.e. preparing the Impugned Wills) and that “these
duties” were owed to Norman, David and Barbara.

Additionally, Mr. Miller failed to make sufficient inquiries to
discover his father's previous promises to David, the mutual wills agreement or
his father's true intentions when he prepared the Impugned Wills, and failed to
warn his father as to the practical consequences of the dispositions in the
Impugned Wills.

e)

Mr. Miller and members of the PGT staff did
certain things “improperly and unfairly and in breach of their common law duty
and fiduciary responsibilities” to David, Barbara and Norman that “flow to
David as a beneficiary” for which he seeks damages for negligence and breach of
fiduciary duty.  Following this allegation are 21 paragraphs of accusations of
improper or self‑interested conduct on the part of one or other of Mr. Miller,
the staff of the PGT and the Attorney General that David claims caused him harm
and induced his father to dispose of his estate contrary to the entrenched agreements
and promises he had made to his wife and son.

[
36
]

Part 2 of the Counterclaim lists 17 paragraphs of
the relief sought by David.  Put broadly, he seeks declarations that the Impugned
Wills are void on multiple grounds and that Norman's 2007 will be declared his
last valid and subsisting will such that Norman's entire estate passes to David
outright, or alternatively, that the entire estate devolves to him on an
intestacy.  David asks for a declaration that he is beneficially entitled to
the Family Residence and an order that title be vested in him absolutely.  He
also seeks compensation in respect of the legal costs he will have incurred in
successfully disputing the validity of the Impugned Wills.

[
37
]

Further, David seeks injunctive relief to enjoin
the PGT from probating the Impugned Wills.

[
38
]

In the event that the Impugned Wills are upheld,
David seeks the following remedies:

a)

Variation of the Impugned Wills so as to
transfer the Family Residence and all other estate property to him unencumbered
by a discretionary trust, or otherwise varied to permit him to live in the
Family Residence for the remainder of his life.

b)

Alternatively, damages from Mr. Miller, the
PGT and the Attorney General in the amount of $1.2 million for their “negligence
and breach of fiduciary duty” flowing from the untrue and misleading comments,
statements and/or representations they made to Norman about David, the
circumstances and/or the effect of the dispositions contained in the Impugned
Wills, with the intent that Norman would rely and act upon such falsehoods.  On
this basis, David asserts that the PGT's misconduct and failure to act in good
faith and with fidelity disentitles it to charge any fees.

To the extent
that Mr. Miller is found to be negligent or in breach of a fiduciary duty owed
to David as a beneficiary, the PGT and the Attorney General are also
responsible for these damages as Mr. Miller was “working on behalf of the PGT”
and acting under their “control and/or as their agent”.

c)

Similar allegations are made in respect of Minister
Taylor and “various people working on the behalf of the Church”, in that they negligently
made false and misleading statements to Norman and exerted pressure upon him so
as to cause David damage, for which he seeks $1.2 million in damages.

d)

Lastly, David requests general damages against
all of the defendants by counterclaim for the infliction of mental suffering.

DISCUSSION

•

Application to Strike the Response and
Counterclaim

[
39
]

The applicants rely on

Rule 9–5(1) of the

SCCR
.
It provides that, at any stage of the proceeding, the Court may
order that the whole or any part of the pleading or other document be struck or
amended on the ground that:

a)

it discloses no reasonable claim or defence, as
the case may be;

b)

it is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or
vexatious;

c)

it may prejudice, embarrass or delay the fair
trial of the proceeding; or

d)

it is otherwise an abuse of the process of the
court.

[
40
]

Where one or more of the grounds enumerated in
Rule 9-5(1) are made out, the Court may pronounce judgment or order that the
proceeding be stayed or dismissed, and that the costs of the application be
paid as special costs.

[
41
]

The
raison d’
ê
tre
of Rule 9-5(1) is as a mechanism to enforce the rules of pleadings:

Doyle Construction Co. v. Carling O’Keefe Breweries of Canada Ltd.
,

1988 CanLII 2843 (BC CA)
, [1988] B.C.J. No. 831, 27 B.C.L.R (2d) 81 (C.A.) [
Doyle
].

[
42
]

The paramount function of pleadings is to define
the issues of fact and law with clarity and precision, in order to give the
opposing party fair notice of the case to be met at trial.  Equally important is
that by defining the essential contours of the case, pleadings facilitate useful
pretrial case management, establish the parameters of pretrial discovery and disclosure,
and determine the necessity and scope of expert opinions:
Keene v. British
Columbia (Ministry of Children and Family Development) & Others
,
2003
BCSC 1544
;
Sahyoun v. Ho
,
2013 BCSC 1143
[
Sahyoun
].

[
43
]

Pleadings are not a vehicle to outline a
detailed narrative of the facts and events that may have bearing upon the case.
Evidence is not to be included:
Sahyoun
at para.
29
; Rule 3-7(1).  Rather,
pleadings must be summary in nature, setting out a concise and orderly statement
of the material facts that give rise to the claim (or counterclaim), establish
a defence, or relate to matters raised by the claim:
Doerksen v. First Open
Heart Society of British Columbia,

2010 BCSC 1291
.

[
44
]

Material facts are the facts that are essential
to formulate each cause of action or defence; no averment crucial to success should
be omitted:
Pyke v. Price Waterhouse Ltd.
,
40 C.P.C. (3d) 7, 1995
CarswellBC 907 (S.C.)
;
Delaney & Friends Cartoon Productions Ltd. v.
Radical Entertainment Inc. et al
,
2005 BCSC 371
;
Skybridge Investments
Ltd. v. Metro Motors Ltd.
,
2006 BCCA 500
;
Young v. Borzoni et al
,
2007
BCCA 16
at para.
20
.

[
45
]

It is the expectation that material facts will
be stated succinctly and with precision, and also be organized in a way that
informs the Court of the issues of fact and law it is being called upon to
decide:
Homalko Indian Band v. British Columbia
,
1998 CanLII 6658 (BC SC)
, [1998] B.C.J.
No. 2703, 25 C.P.C. (4th) 107 (S.C.);
Glenayre Manufacturing v. Pilot
Pacific Properties, et al
,
2003 BCSC 303
.

[
46
]

Particulars and material facts are different in
their character and purpose.  Broadly speaking, particulars are intended to
limit the generality of the pleadings and the issues to be tried; enable the
other side to properly prepare for trial; tie the hands of the party supplying
the particulars; and inform the opposing party what the pleader intends to
prove, as distinct from the mode in which the case is to be proved:
Cansulex
Ltd. v. Perry
,
1982 CarswellBC 836 (C.A.)
.  They should follow the material
facts and be identified as such.  Although particulars must supply sufficient
detail of the case to be met, they are not to include the evidence that is  anticipated
will be adduced at trial to prove the pleaded facts.

[
47
]

The distinctions between evidence and material
facts, and between evidence and particulars can be difficult to draw in
practice.  Despite the challenges, the integrity of those lines must be maintained
as stringently as is reasonably possible.

[
48
]

Where a party pleads a legal conclusion such as,
for example, the existence of a duty of care or of a fiduciary duty, sufficient
material facts must be pleaded to support that conclusion:
Ferstay v.
Dywidag Systems International
,
2008 BCSC 793
; Rule 3‑7(9).

[
49
]

Where, as in the case at hand, there are
allegations of fraud, breach of trust, undue influence and misrepresentation,
inclusion of full particulars, including the dates and items as they are known
at the time of the pleading, are mandatory: Rule 3‑7(18).

[
50
]

Rule 9‑5(2) confirms that no evidence is
admissible on an application brought to strike a pleading on the ground that it
does not disclose a reasonable claim or defence.  The facts are to be taken as
pleaded.  Evidence is admissible, however, in relation to the other grounds.

[
51
]

In
Citizens for

Foreign Aid Reform
Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,
1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, 36 C.P.C. (4th) 266, 1999 CarswellBC 2111
(S.C.), Romilly J. provided an overview of the key principles that inform the
analysis of whether a pleading ought to be struck under the predecessor to sub-rules
9-5(1)(b) and (c) at para. 47:

[47]      Irrelevancy
and embarrassment are both established when pleadings are so confusing that it
is difficult to understand what is being pleaded:
Gittings v. Caneco
Audio-Publishers Inc.
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2561 (BC SC)
, 17 B.C.L.R. (2d) 38 (B.C.S.C.). An
“embarrassing” and “scandalous” pleading is one that is so irrelevant that it
will involve the parties in useless expense and will prejudice the trial of the
action by involving them in a dispute apart from the issues:
Keddie v. Dumas
Hotels Ltd
. (1985),
1985 CanLII 417 (BC CA)
, 62 B.C.L.R. 145 at 147 (B.C.C.A.).  An
allegation which is scandalous will not be struck if it is relevant to the
proceedings.  It will only be struck if irrelevant as well as scandalous:
College
of Dental Surgeons of B.C. v. Cleland
, (1968),
1968 CanLII 1008 (BC CA)
, 66 W.W.R. 499
(B.C.C.A.).  A pleading is “unnecessary” or “vexatious” if it does not go
to establishing the plaintiff’s cause of action or does not advance any claim
known in law:
Strauts v. Harrigan
,
1992 CanLII 595 (BC SC)
, [1992] B.C.J. No. 86
(Q.L.) (B.C.S.C.).  A pleading that is superfluous will not be struck out
if it is not necessarily unnecessary or otherwise objectionable:
Lutz v.
Canadian Puget Sound Lumber and Timber Co.
(1920), 28 B.C.R 39
(C.A.)
.  A pleading is “frivolous” if it is obviously unsustainable, not
in the sense that it lacks an evidentiary basis, but because of the doctrine of
estoppel
: Chrisgian v. B.C. Rail Ltd. et al.
(6 July 1992),
Prince George Registry 20714 (B.C.S.C.).

[
52
]

A pleading may be embarrassing or scandalous
within the contemplation of the Rule where it: does not state the real issues
in an intelligible form; is overly prolix; includes irrelevant facts; is
calculated to confuse the opposing party and make it difficult, and perhaps impossible,
to answer; or contains arguments or evidence:
Kuhn v. American Credit Indemnity
Co.
,
[1992] B.C.J. No. 953 (S.C.)
;
McNutt v. A.G. Canada et al.
,

2004 BCSC 1113
at para.
41
;
B.C./Yukon Association of Drug War
Survivors v. Abbotsford (City)
,
2014 BCSC 1817
at paras.
93-94
;
Spillane
v. United Parcel Service Canada Ltd. et al
,
2006 BCSC 687
at para.
22
;

Budgell v. British Columbia
,
2007 BCSC 991
at para.
20
.

[
53
]

That being said, so long as the pleadings do not
confuse the opposing party or make it difficult for that party to understand
the case that must be met, sheer verbosity does not ordinarily provide sufficient
justification for striking a claim:
Doyle

at para.
4
;
347202
B.C. Ltd. v. Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce
,
[1995] B.C.J. No. 449
(S.C.)
;
Stanley v. KCL West Holdings Inc. et al
,
2004 BCSC 1555
.

[
54
]

A crucial consideration in determining whether to
strike a pleading under Rule 9‑5(1)(a) is whether it can be preserved by
amendment:
International

Taoist Church Canada v. Ching Chung Taoist
Association of Hong Kong Limited
,
2011 BCCA 149
.  The prospect of
rectifying deficient pleadings by way of amendment is also a factor in
considering whether the pleading ought to be struck on the other grounds:
Ahmed
v. Assu
,
2014 BCSC 1768
;
Willow v. Chong
,
2013 BCSC 1083
at para.
23
.

[
55
]

Turning now to David’s pleadings, as I have
mentioned, voluminous pieces of evidence and argument punctuate much of the Response
in the guise of material facts or particulars.  That pleading is plainly
embarrassing within the contemplation of the Rule for this reason alone.

[
56
]

The manner in which David has expressed a number
of his allegations in each pleading make it difficult to fully grasp the scope
and nature of his claims.  In order to discern them completely, the opposing
parties would have had little choice but to pour over the pleadings with
careful attention to the cross‑references and the overlapping averments of
facts and to construe the sometimes vague references to the constituent
elements of legal concepts.  The allegations of undue influence, pressure,
untrue statements and suggestions on the part of various of the parties illustrate
this point.

[
57
]

The concept of undue influence in relation to
the procurement of a will or testamentary gift is a species of constructive
fraud and is tantamount to coercion.  Yet, in addition to claiming undue
influence, David pleads several allegations to the effect that certain of the
defendants by Counterclaim and “various people" acting on behalf of the
Church, exerted pressure or made improper or untrue suggestions, statements or
representations to Norman.  On their face, these plainly fall short of material
facts that would support a claim of undue influence at law.  To the extent that
David has attempted to articulate these claims within the confines of
recognized legal concepts, or to particularize them, the overall result is a
rambling and disjointed composition.  It is not always clear what actionable
wrong is being alleged; is it undue influence or misrepresentation, or both, or
something different altogether?  A deficiency on the other side of the same
coin can be found in paragraph 48.1 of the Response.  There, David alleges that
the Impugned Wills are the result of duress and undue influence, but fails to
identify who is responsible for such misconduct.

[
58
]

Further examples of inexplicit content abound in
relation to the claims made against Mr. Miller, which are complex and interwoven
with other claims.  By way of example, David alleges that Mr. Miller (and
others) owed a fiduciary and a common law duty to David as the sole beneficiary
of his father's estate, and in breach of such duties, caused Norman to make
certain dispositions in the Impugned Wills.  He accuses Mr. Miller of
bringing a degree of improper pressure or influence to bear upon Norman's
decision‑making relative to David, and of “urging, promoting or
instructing” Norman to dispose of his property in a manner contrary to his previously
stated intentions, his promises to David and his agreement with Barbara to not
revoke his 2007 will.  David further alleges that Mr. Miller permitted
Norman to give instructions with respect to the Impugned Wills while Norman was
under duress and/or lacking testamentary capacity.  It is not sufficiently
clear as to which of these allegations are components of David’s larger undue
influence claim and which of them relate to one or more independent claims
against Mr. Miller.  The pleadings pertaining to these subject areas are
muddled and lack cohesion and many recite evidence and argument.  They are
plainly embarrassing.

[
59
]

I share Mr. Miller's assessment that
David’s allegations of misrepresentation against Mr. Miller are similarly
defective.  Assuming that the allegations of false statements and
misrepresentations made to his father by Mr. Miller are intended to ground
an independent cause of action founded on negligent or fraudulent
misrepresentation (a point that itself requires clarification, as I have said),
he omits any averment to the effect that he was aware of and relied upon such
misstatements.  Reliance is an essential ingredient of actionable
misrepresentation:
Proprietary Industries Inc. v. CIBC World Markets Inc.
,

2002 BCSC 999
.  In addition, particulars of the alleged misrepresentations have
not been supplied as is required by Rule 3-7(18).

[
60
]

As David’s pleadings presently stand, I am not
confident that I am able to accurately disentangle the various bases that ground
his claims against Mr. Miller.  By way of example, the allegation contained in
paragraph 16.1 of the Counterclaim, by which he purports to assert a duty owed
to him by Mr. Miller, is a convoluted pleading.  It does not explicitly allege
that Mr. Miller was ever retained by David.  Moreover, it does not state
the material facts that could give rise to a duty of care in David's favour.  This
too is an embarrassing plea and, in its current form, discloses no reasonable claim.

[
61
]

To the extent that one of David’s foundations is
that Mr. Miller owed him a duty as a beneficiary under his father's 2007 will to,
in effect, not carry out Norman's instructions that were inconsistent with the
provisions of that will, it is doomed to fail:
Korpiel v. Sanguinetti
,

[1999] B.C.J. No. 1048 (S.C.)
;
Graham v. Bonnycastle
,
2004 ABCA
270
, leave to appeal to S.C.C. ref’d [2004] S.C.C.A. No. 489.  Insofar as that
has been pleaded by David, it must be and is hereby struck to that extent as
there is plainly no reasonable claim on that ground.

[
62
]

David’s allegation of negligent infliction of
mental distress also appears flawed in its current form.  In the first place,
it is questionable as to whether the anguish and suffering David alleges he
experienced would meet the threshold of severe psychological injury that is
compensable under this tort:
Mustapha v. Culligan of Canada Ltd.
,
2008
SCC 27
[
Mustapha
].  Moreover, David has not alleged any material facts
to demonstrate that the psychological harm he suffered was a reasonably foreseeable
consequence of the negligent conduct, which is a further compulsory element of
the tort:
Mustapha

at para.
18
;
Dhillon v. Jaffer
,
2014 BCCA 215
.

[
63
]

Citing
Easingwood v. Cockroft
,
2011 BCSC
1154
[
Easingwood
], Mr. Miller contends that David's allegation that
the Impugned Wills constitute fraudulent conveyances under the
FCA
is
ill-conceived because a will can never be a fraudulent conveyance.  In my
opinion, Mr. Miller’s submission is constructed on an overly narrow reading of
Easingwood
.
Collectively, the authorities, including
Easingwood
,
support the
proposition that an individual who has a legal or equitable claim against a
person, prior to that person's death (that is to say, a claim other than a
wills variation claim), may have standing as a “creditor or other” to launch a
claim under the
FCA
: see generally,
Antrobus v. Antrobus
,
2009
BCSC 1341
;
Mawdsley v. Meshen
,
2010 BCSC 1099
, aff’d
2012 BCCA 91
.  As
to whether this proposition applies where the impugned disposition is
testamentary in nature is an issue worthy of judicial consideration.  On the
case law, it cannot be said that David’s allegations in this regard are plainly
and obviously bound to fail.   On the other hand, however, David’s bald
assertions that the Impugned Wills are void as being against public policy, for
reasons unrelated to his claim under the
FCA
are built on tenuous legal underpinnings
and are problematic.

[
64
]

In the circumstances, I am prepared to allow
David a reasonable opportunity to appropriately streamline his pleadings and
make the amendments required to rectify the multiple deficiencies.  I am not
persuaded that permitting him to reform his pleadings by way of substantial
amendments would result in any more confusion or ambiguity of the real issues
or otherwise be prejudicial to the other parties.  The exception to this is the
order I have made above in paragraph 61 by which I have struck one of David’s
claims as hopeless in law.

[
65
]

It is unduly burdensome for the Court to perform
a forensic evaluation of David's pleadings, approving or disapproving of them
line-by-line.  This is especially true where, as here, the applicants have not
themselves audited the pleadings with that level of intense scrutiny.  Nor is
it the role of the Court to rewrite David's pleadings for him, and I do not
propose to do so.  Rather, I have drawn counsel’s attention to the main
legal principles at play and have identified the most significant deficiencies.
I am confident this will provide sufficient judicial direction to counsel as
to the nature of the amendments required.

[
66
]

David’s counsel has until August 31, 2016 to
amend the Response and the Counterclaim.

•

Application to Sever and Stay

[
67
]

Rules 22-5(6) and (7) state:

Separation

(6)        If
a joinder of several claims or parties in a proceeding may unduly complicate or
delay the trial or hearing of the proceeding or is otherwise inconvenient, the
court may order separate trials or hearings or make any other order it
considers will further the object of these
Supreme Court Civil Rules
.

Separating counterclaim or third party
claims

(7)        If a
counterclaim or a third party proceeding ought to be disposed of by a separate
proceeding, the court may so order.

[
68
]

The key factors engaged in a general sense on an
application to sever were canvassed in
Schaper v. Sears Canada
,
2000
BCSC 1575
[
Schaper
] at para.
19
:

1.         ...the
party making the request must show that hearing the claims together would
unduly complicate, delay the hearing, or otherwise be inconvenient. If a party
applying does not meet this threshold, the court need not go further in any
analysis and the application should be dismissed.

2.         Have
the actions of any party in the proceeding been unreasonable and have they
contributed to the complication, the delay, or the inconvenience alleged by the
party applying? If this found, that would strengthen the argument to sever.

3.         Are
the issues between the plaintiff and defendant and the issues between the
defendant and the third party sufficiently distinct so as to allow them to be
tried separately? If so, that strengthens the argument to sever off third party
proceeding.

4.         Is
the relief claimed by, or the potential obligation of, any party best
determined by hearing the evidence of all parties at one hearing? If so, that
weakens an application to sever.

5.         Does the
prejudice to the party applying, prejudice based on undue complication, delay
or inconvenience, outweigh any benefit of matters being heard together, or
outweigh any considerations related to the overall objective of the rules to
ensure a just, speedy and inexpensive determination of every proceeding on its
merits, including the avoidance of a multiplicity of proceedings for the
benefits of litigants and having concern to congestion in the courts generally?

[
69
]

Guidelines that focused attention more keenly on
the efficacy of the trial process were helpfully laid out in
O’Mara v. Son,

Kim et al.
,
2007 BCSC 871
[
O’Mara
] at para.
23
:

1.         whether the order sought will
create a saving in pre-trial procedures;

2.         whether
there will be a real reduction in the number of trial days taken up by the
trial being heard at the same trial;

3.         whether
a party may be seriously inconvenienced by being required to attend a trial in
which the party may have a marginal interest;

4.         whether
there will be a real saving in expert’s time and witness fees;

5.         whether
one of the actions is at a more advanced stage than the other;

6.         whether
the order sought will result in delay of the trial of any one of the actions
and, if so, whether any prejudice which a party might suffer as a result of
that delay outweighs the potential benefits which a consolidated trial might
otherwise have;

7.         the
possibility of inconsistent findings and common issues resulting from separate
trials.

[
70
]

Severance may well be appropriate where the
determination of one issue will render another one moot:
Lawrence v. ICBC
,

2001 BCSC 1530
[
Lawrence
].

[
71
]

The judicial discretion to sever trials or
hearings is to be exercised sparingly:
Morrison‑Knudsen Co. v. British
Columbia Hydro & Power Authority
,
1972 CanLII 992 (BC SC)
, 1972 Carswell B.C. 62, 24 D.L.R. (3d)
579 (S.C.);
Lawrence

at

para.
43
. The test for severance is not
applied in a vacuum; it is to be considered against the backdrop of the nature
of the particular case at hand:
Wirtz v. Constantini
,
1982 CanLII 282 (BC SC)
, 137 D.L.R. (3d)
393, 1982 CarswellBC 588 (S.C.).  Because the determination involves an
individualized assessment of the unique case before the Court, there is no
closed list of uniformly applied considerations that inform the exercise of the
Court’s discretion.

[
72
]

David asserts that the significant overlap of the
parties and of the potential witnesses in relation to his various claims render
it uneconomic and greatly prejudicial to him if the causes of action are severed

off and litigated separately.  As I understand it, he further contends that
because the Impugned Wills were made in violation of the binding agreement and/or
trust between his parents that underlies the 2007 Wills and the promises made
to him and therefore constitute a breach of trust, breach of contract, and/or
fraudulent conveyances, they should not be submitted for probate in the first
place.  It is his position that the foregoing issues should be adjudicated upon
before the validity of the Impugned Wills is decided or, alternatively, at the
same time.

[
73
]

Mutual wills refer to the mirror-image or
reciprocal wills of two persons (usually spouses) who have made a binding
agreement (as distinct from a loose understanding or engagement of honour) to
structure their wills in a certain manner and to not alter or revoke them
without the other's consent, or that any subsequent will they make would adhere
to the original agreed scheme of distribution:
Edell v. Sitzer
(2001),
2001 CanLII 27989 (ON SC)
, 55
O.R. (3d) 198 (Sup. Ct. J.), aff’d (2004),
2004 CanLII 654 (ON CA)
, 187 O.A.C. 189, leave to appeal to
S.C.C. ref’d [2004] S.C.C.A. No. 372.

[
74
]

In the context of mutual wills, the concept of
an underlying agreement not to revoke one’s will is somewhat misleading.  This
is because it is well‑settled that such an agreement does not deprive the
parties of the right to revoke their wills:
Hall v. McLaughlin Estate
,

[2006] O.J. No. 2848, 25 E.T.R. (3d) 198 (Sup. Ct. J.) [
Hall
]
.  A
will can always be revoked: see generally,
University of Manitoba v.
Sanderson Estate
(1998),
1998 CanLII 4328 (BC CA)
, 155 D.L.R. (4th) 40 (B.C.C.A.) [
University of
Manitoba
].  The weight of the jurisprudence holds that, in the result, the
probate court does not concern itself with an agreement not to revoke a will:
Re
Heys
, [1914] P. 192.  In other words, that a will may have been made
in violation of a mutual wills agreement not to revoke does not preclude the
offending will from being admitted to probate in common or solemn form.
However, a proven breach of the agreement may well give rise to an action for
damages in contract or be remedied by the imposition of a constructive trust on
the subject property:
University of Manitoba
;
Synge v. Synge
,
[1894]
1 Q.B. 466 (C.A.)
;
Re Green
,
[1951] Ch. 148, [1950] 2 All E.R. 913
;
Hall
.

[
75
]

Appreciation of these principles forcefully undercuts
David's submission that the issue of the mutual wills ought to be adjudicated
before or at the same time as the validity of the Impugned Wills.  His companion
assertion, which was not well‑developed, that his claim under the
FCA

should proceed before or together with the Proof of Will Action, suffers the
same fate.

[
76
]

Mr. Miller's counsel asserts that the most
of David's claims, other than those encompassed in the Proof of Will Action,
cannot be litigated until a representative of Norman's estate has been determined
and a grant of probate or administration, as the case may be, has issued.  At
first blush, that submission appears to be at odds with the plain language of

s. 24(1)
of the
PPA
:

Death of patient

24
(1)
Subject to subsection (2), on the death of a patient and until a representation
grant, within the meaning of the
Wills, Estates and Succession Act
, is
issued in respect of the patient's estate and notice in writing of the
representation grant is served on the committee, the committee of the patient

(a) continues to have the rights,
powers, duties and privileges that the committee would have had if the patient
had not died, and

(b) has the powers of a person who
has been issued a representation grant.

[
77
]

There is no question but that as the executor
named in the Impugned Wills, the PGT is entitled to bring the Proof of Will
Action.  On the surface,
s. 24
of the
PPA

suggests that in its
capacity as committee of Norman’s estate, the PGT would have the authority to
defend against the other claims.  However, in
Re: Langford and The Patients
Property Act
,
2000 BCSC 721
[
Re: Langford
], the Court reasoned that
the legislature could not have intended to invest a committee with all of the
powers of an executor or administrator such as obtaining title to the
deceased’s assets or winding up and distributing the estate of the deceased
patient.  It held that because
s. 24
expressly contemplates that probate
or administration will be taken out after a patient's death, it is intended to
be operative only in the intervening period.  In the result,
Re: Langford
held
that
s. 24
simply authorizes a committee of a deceased patient to maintain
the
status quo
of the deceased patient’s estate during the hiatus period
pending the issuance of letters probate or administration.

[
78
]

The proposition established in
Re: Langford

raises a legitimate question concerning the PGT’s authority to represent the interests
of Norman’s estate in litigation beyond the Proof of Will Action.  This
bolsters the applicants’ position that it is preferable to separate the Proof
of Will Action from the other claims and try it first.

[
79
]

Another layer of complexity is that David has
levied serious allegations against the PGT in its corporate capacity, as
opposed to its capacity as the named executor of the Impugned Wills or as
Norman’s representative
qua
committee.  Trying all of the claims
together may place the PGT in a conflict of interest as between its role as the
putative executor and Norman’s committee on the one hand, and its self‑interest
on the other.  That may, in turn, necessitate the appointment of a separate
litigation representative of Norman’s estate in respect of the claims other
than the Proof of Will Action.  These considerations also militate for
severance.

[
80
]

The PGT asserts that, when sitting as a court of
probate, this Court is confined to adjudicating issues bearing directly on the
validity of the Impugned Wills, namely whether Norman had testamentary
capacity, acted of his own volition and duly executed the Impugned Wills with
knowledge and approval of their contents.   Relying on
Ali Estate (Re)
,

2011 BCSC 537
[
Ali
], the PGT contends that that those of David’s claims that
fall outside the narrow ambit of a proof in solemn form action, must be pursued
in a separate proceeding.

[
81
]

Ali
was not a
proof of will in solemn form case.  It involved an application to rectify a
will by adding words and, failing that, to construe a particular clause in the
same will.  The essential point of
Ali
, instructively made by Dardi J.,
was that this Court has historically exercised its probate and construction of
will functions in separate proceedings.  Endorsing the maintenance of those
dual jurisdictions, her Ladyship held that when sitting as a court of probate,
the Court has no jurisdiction to add words to a will; it was able to do so only
while sitting as a court of construction.  In the course of her analysis, Madam
Justice Dardi observed that the issues before the court of probate typically
focus on what constitutes the testamentary instrument of the will-maker and its
validity.

[
82
]

In my view, the PGT seeks to extend the narrow proposition
established in
Ali
beyond its intended limits.  It is particularly
noteworthy that the discrete question before Dardi J. made it unnecessary to
consider the broader question of the existence and extent of any limitations of
the issues that might be joined in a proof of will case in light of the
SCCR

and the jurisprudence that applies to joinder and the claims that can be
properly litigated in a counterclaim.

[
83
]

That being said, there is case authority that
has placed some limitation on the nature of claims that can properly be included
in a counterclaim to a proof of will in solemn form proceeding.  In
Clark v.
Nash
,
[1986] B.C.J. No. 1655 (S.C.)
aff’d
[1987] B.C.J. No. 304 (C.A.) [
Clark
]
,
the Court held that the procedure and hearing involved in a proof of will in
solemn form proceeding should be limited to the aspects of the will execution, testamentary
capacity, want of knowledge and fraud.  The Court reasoned that a counterclaim
to vary a will that is alleged to be invalid is therefore premature, and
hearing it at the same time or before the action involving the proof of the challenged
will is neither just nor convenient.

[
84
]

Since its pronouncement,
Clark
has stood
for the general proposition that it is improper to include a wills variation
claim in an action for proof of will in solemn form on the footing that a valid
will is a condition precedent to a variation proceeding.  Although I believe
that, on occasion, this Court has heard such claims together (presumably
without being taken to
Clark
),
Clark
nonetheless strengthens the
application to sever, at least
vis-a-vis
David’s claim to have the
Impugned Wills varied.

[
85
]

The validity of the Impugned Wills is the
centerpiece issue of this litigation.  If they are not valid, David will
inherit the entirety of his father's estate, including the Family Residence, in
one of two ways: either pursuant to his father’s 2007 will or by application of
the laws of intestate succession.  In either scenario, substantially all of
David’s other claims will fall by the wayside, leaving no claim to advance,
except possibly for the negligent infliction of mental suffering and to recover
the legal costs David incurred in successfully defending the Proof of Will
Action.  These factors also weigh in favour of severing the Proof of Will
Action from the balance of David’s claims.

[
86
]

In turning my mind to the considerations
outlined in
Schaper
and
O’Mara
and the other factors germane to
the analysis, I conclude that, while features of the factual matrix are
relevant to the Proof of Will Action and David’s other claims, the issues are
not so tightly interconnected as to make separate trials, at different times
and before different judges, fraught with extra expense or inefficiencies, or
overly prejudicial to David.  The issues relevant to the Proof of Will Action
are sufficiently distinct from the issues raised in David’s remaining claims.

[
87
]

In my view, significant judicial economy and proportionality
will be achieved by litigating the Proof of Will Action first and separately
from all of David’s other claims, which far outweighs any prejudice visited
upon David in so doing.  Examined from another perspective but to the same end,
hearing all of the claims together would unduly complicate and delay the
proceeding.  Trial fairness and convenience support severance of the Proof of
Will Action from the balance of David’s claims.

[
88
]

For clarity, the Proof of Will Action incorporates
the following issues:

a)

whether Norman had the requisite testamentary
capacity to validly make one or both of the Impugned Wills (which encompasses
the issue of whether any surrounding suspicious circumstances existed) and whether
he knew and approved of the contents of the Impugned Wills;

b)

whether the Norman’s instructions and execution
of the Impugned Wills were free from delusions and undue influence; and

c)

whether the Impugned Wills were validly executed
in accordance with the formal requirements pursuant to the
Wills Act
.

[
89
]

I do not share the view urged by the PGT that
Powell
v. Powell
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2544 (BC SC)
, 21 B.C.L.R. (2d) 109 (S.C.) or Rule 25-14 precludes from
consideration in the Proof of Will Action, David's claim that his father’s last
valid and subsisting will is the one that he executed on February 22, 2007.  That
claim is also properly before the Court in the Proof of Will Action.

[
90
]

Mr. Miller asks that all of the claims
against him be severed from the others, and that they be stayed until all such
claims have been determined.  His rationale is that the existence and nature of
any claims against him cannot be known and will not arise until the other
claims have been determined.  Depending on the outcome of such claims, it is
possible there will be no claim to bring against him.  He also highlights that
the claims against him are in the nature of solicitor’s negligence and contends
that it is therefore not appropriate they be joined with the other claims.

[
91
]

In addition to the Court’s jurisdiction to order
that claims be stayed under Rule 9‑5(1), it may temporarily stay a proceeding
pursuant to its inherent jurisdiction or
s. 8(2)
of the
Law and Equity
Act
, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 253, or both:
Zurich Indemnity Co. of Canada
v. Western Delta Lands Inc.
,
[1997] B.C.J. No. 1784 at para. 14
(C.A.)
, leave to appeal to S.C.C. ref’d [1997] S.C.C.A. No. 469 [
Zurich
].
In exercising its discretion to grant or deny a stay, the Court must weigh the
potential benefits and prejudice at play and fairly balance the parties’
competing interests.

[
92
]

In circumstances where findings in a related
action will likely substantially narrow or simplify the claims that are sought
to be stayed, a common judicial approach is to try the claims separately and
sequentially and to temporarily stay the dependant claims pending the
resolution of the first:
Zurich
;
Peh v. The Owners, Strata Plan LMS
3837
,
2008 BCSC 291
at paras.
61-67
;
Ainsworth Lumber Co. v. A.G.
of Canada,
2001 BCCA 105
[
Ainsworth
] at paras.
5-14
.  That the
stay being sought is only temporary also supports the granting of one:
Ainsworth

at para.
10
.

[
93
]

In their present form, the allegations against
Mr. Miller are deeply intertwined with allegations against other parties and aver
to misconduct on the part of Mr. Miller that may extend beyond ordinary
solicitor’s negligence.  As the claims are currently pleaded, I am concerned
that separating those against Mr. Miller from the remainder carries too great a
risk of prejudice to David for too small a benefit to Mr. Miller and the trial
process.

[
94
]

Accordingly, at his juncture I am not prepared
to exercise my discretion to separate the claims against Mr. Miller from all
others.  I have ordered that the Proof of Will Action is to be tried separately
and proceed first.  All other claims are to be stayed until the Proof of Will
Action has been determined.  Once the outcome of the Proof of Will Action is
known, Mr. Miller is at liberty to re‑apply for severance of the claims
against him from those then outstanding and may revive his application for
special costs.

OTHER MATTERS

[
95
]

This case may be well‑served by judicial
case management.  If counsel have not already done so, I invite them to apply
for the assignment of a Case Management Judge at their first opportunity.

[
96
]

The applicants have been substantially
successful and are entitled to their costs payable by David in any event of the
cause.

“Ballance J.”
